headline: Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir elected President of Bangladesh, as widely anticipated
summary: The former BNP Secretary-General's appointment was not a surprise, given his widespread respect and the established practice of selecting a party nominee.
details: Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir has been elected President of Bangladesh, a development that came as no surprise. His name had frequently been mentioned as the BNP's nominee for the presidency since the election.

He is widely regarded as a gentleman and respected figure, even outside his party. While the President's role in Bangladesh is largely ceremonial and routine, it can become crucial during special circumstances and crises, requiring the President to rise above party lines.

Routine duties include delivering speeches in Parliament at least once a year and after a new parliament is elected. The President also receives credentials from new foreign ambassadors, a mandatory protocol.

On various national days, the President's responsibilities increase, including laying wreaths at the Shaheed Minar or National Memorial. Additionally, the President issues messages on these national occasions and sometimes travels abroad, particularly for state funerals.

A common practice in Bangladesh is for the President to travel abroad for medical treatment every six to twelve months. Past presidents have undertaken such trips with large entourages, and observers will note the size of Mirza Fakhrul's delegation.

The President's most significant duty is to assent to bills passed by Parliament. While the constitution allows the President to send a bill back for reconsideration, this risk is rarely taken by Bangladeshi presidents.

Given his extensive experience as the Secretary-General of BNP, handling the routine presidential duties will not be difficult for him. The nation can trust his experience and wisdom to manage any potential crises, should they arise.

However, the presidential role is not as straightforward as it might appear. Presidents often become isolated in Bangabhaban, losing direct contact with political dynamics and party activities due to strict protocols.

Historical examples, such as the removal of Badruddoza Chowdhury and the challenges faced by Iajuddin Ahmed during the One-Eleven period, highlight the political vulnerability of a president. They often find themselves in a helpless position.

Mirza Fakhrul Islam is not known for a large ego or excessive protocol. It is expected that he will maintain a harmonious relationship with the government and party leaders, upholding the dignity and protocols of the presidential office.

headline_marked: [[PM picks up Ehsanul Huda in car]] during Kishoreganj visit, sparking new debate in Bajitpur BNP politics
headline: PM picks up Ehsanul Huda in car during Kishoreganj visit, sparking new debate in Bajitpur BNP politics
summary: During the Prime Minister's visit to Kishoreganj, she picked up Syed Ehsanul Huda, who recently joined BNP, in her car. This incident, coupled with the absence of rival BNP leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, has sparked new discussions within Bajitpur's divided BNP
details: During the Prime Minister's recent visit to Kishoreganj, she notably picked up Syed Ehsanul Huda in her car. This occurred while Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, the Member of Parliament for Kishoreganj-5 (Bajitpur-Nikli) constituency, was absent from the area. Photos and videos of the incident quickly spread on social media, igniting fresh discussions about the divided politics of the BNP in Bajitpur.

The incident has become a major talking point among leaders and activists of the two factions within the Bajitpur Upazila BNP. Ehsanul Huda's followers interpret it as a significant indication of his central standing within the party. Conversely, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's supporters argue that being in the Prime Minister's car should not be seen as a measure of local political leadership.

The BNP's politics in Bajitpur has been split into two factions since the 13th national parliamentary election, primarily over party nominations. One faction is led by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, the expelled president of the Upazila BNP. The other is led by Syed Ehsanul Huda, who was the BNP candidate for the same constituency and lost the election.

Sheikh Mujibur Rahman initially sought the BNP nomination and was even given a primary nomination. However, Syed Ehsanul Huda later joined the BNP in December 2025, after dissolving his father's Bangladesh Jatiya Dal, and was subsequently given the final nomination for the seat.

Despite not receiving the party nomination, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman contested the election as an independent candidate. He went on to defeat Ehsanul Huda, the BNP's 'Dhannyer Shish' (sheaf of paddy) candidate, by a margin of 13,154 votes, becoming the Member of Parliament.

For defying the party's decision and participating in the election, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was expelled from the BNP on January 24 of this year. Eighty-three other leaders from Bajitpur and Nikli Upazilas who supported him were also expelled for the same reason. Despite their expulsion, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and his followers remained active in local politics, organizing various programs under the banner of the Upazila BNP.

Anticipation grew among both factions after the Prime Minister's Kishoreganj visit was announced on August 16. Both sides held multiple preparatory meetings, attempting to demonstrate their strength. Mujibur Rahman's supporters had expected him to be on the Prime Minister's stage, with Ehsanul Huda below, and rumors even circulated about a positive message regarding the revocation of expulsion orders.

However, the situation changed the night before the visit, on August 15, when news spread on social media that Sheikh Mujibur Rahman had fallen ill. It was later confirmed that he had traveled to Singapore for treatment of a heart-related issue, thus missing the Prime Minister's program on August 16.

Throughout the Prime Minister's program, Ehsanul Huda's followers were actively present in Bajitpur politics, gathering in Katiadi area from morning, dressed in matching t-shirts and caps. Despite earlier talks of a large show of strength from Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's side, they were not seen in significant numbers as a group that day.

Then came the much-discussed incident: the Prime Minister stopped her car upon seeing Ehsanul Huda and invited him inside. Pictures and videos of this moment quickly went viral on social media, adding a new dimension to the divided politics of the BNP in Bajitpur.

Ehsan Kufia, president of Bajitpur Municipal BNP and a leader of Ehsanul Huda's faction, stated, "They said they would be on stage, but what did the public see? The public saw that they were not there, but we were. Not only that, the Prime Minister called Ehsanul Huda and took him into her car. This is not just about getting into a car; it's a big message for the BNP politics of Bajitpur-Nikli."

Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's followers, however, do not view the incident in the same light. Md. Moniruzzaman, the Upazila BNP General Secretary, who was also expelled for supporting Mujibur Rahman, confirmed that Sheikh Mujibur Rahman has a heart condition and had to go to Singapore for urgent treatment. Moniruzzaman commented, "Illness doesn't come with a warning. And someone getting a place in the Prime Minister's car doesn't mean political control is in their hands. Those who are exaggerating this are miscalculating local politics." He also criticized the political exploitation and trolling regarding Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's illness as uncivilized.

Regarding the lower turnout of their activists at the Prime Minister's program, Moniruzzaman explained that the Prime Minister does not want any disorder in her programs, and district leaders had advised activists to remain restrained. He also suggested that the revocation of the expulsion orders was only a matter of time. Mozaffar Rahman, the Organizational Secretary of Bajitpur Upazila BNP, who remains neutral, acknowledged that "one person getting into a car, and another going abroad" are significant topics of discussion in Bajitpur BNP politics.
